kurals.tamil:
சிற்றினம் அஞ்சும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Sitrinam anjum perumai sirumaidhaan
Sutramaach soozhndhu vidum.
kurals.meaning: Greatness fears the company of the mean-minded, but smallness embraces such people and gathers them round as its own kin.
kurals.elementary: A truly great person is careful to stay away from petty, mean-spirited people, almost as if afraid of them. A small-minded person does the opposite: they happily pull those same people close and treat them like family.
kurals.university: Valluvar opens the chapter by defining two temperaments through a single reaction: அஞ்சும் (‘fears, shrinks from’) versus சுற்றமாச் சூழ்ந்து விடும் (‘surrounds itself with them as kinsfolk’). The சிற்றினம் (‘small/mean kind’) are not necessarily criminals; commentators such as Parimelazhagar gloss them as the base-minded whose company slowly lowers one’s own standard. The chiasmus of பெருமை/சிறுமை (greatness/smallness) makes character a matter of affinity: we show what we are by whom we are comfortable with. This chapter is the deliberate counterweight to chapter 45 (பெரியாரைத் துணைக்கோடல, seeking the help of the great): what one should seek there, one should fear here.

hinduism.quote_or_event: The Narada Bhakti Sutra (sutra 43) teaches “duḥsaṅgaḥ sarvathaiva tyājyaḥ” — bad company is to be given up in every way.
hinduism.explanation: In the bhakti tradition, dussanga (evil association) is treated as something the serious seeker must avoid completely, not just keep under control.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘greatness fears mean company’ matches the sutra’s call to avoid bad company in every way; both see keeping away as the mark of a serious, elevated person.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong match; the Sanskrit phrase is standard, but English renderings vary by translator, so it is marked as a paraphrase.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And have no fellowship with the unfruitful works of darkness, but rather reprove them.”
christianity.explanation: Paul tells believers to stay out of partnership with sinful conduct and to expose it instead of joining in.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural, it calls for refusing fellowship with what is base; Paul adds a duty to rebuke, which the Kural does not mention.
christianity._accuracy_note: Aimed at sinful works rather than petty-minded people; the idea of refusing fellowship lines up well.

islam.quote_or_event: “And when you see those who engage in [offensive] discourse concerning Our verses, then turn away from them until they enter into another conversation.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an tells the believer to walk away from gatherings where sacred things are mocked, and not to sit on with them.
islam.tie_back: Getting up and leaving low company is the behaviour the Kural credits to greatness.
islam._accuracy_note: Narrower context (mockery of revelation), but the action of withdrawing from base company is the same.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Blessed is the man that walketh not in the counsel of the ungodly, nor standeth in the way of sinners, nor sitteth in the seat of the scornful.”
judaism.explanation: The first verse of the Psalms defines the blessed person by the company they refuse, moving from walking to standing to sitting with the wicked.
judaism.tie_back: Both texts measure a person’s worth by the company they keep away from.
judaism._accuracy_note: Very close; the ‘scornful’ are a good match for the Kural’s mean-minded.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Do not associate with evil companions; do not seek the fellowship of the vile. Associate with the good friends; seek the fellowship of noble men.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha tells his followers to avoid vile companions and look for noble ones.
buddhism.tie_back: The Pali ‘purisādhame’ (lowest of men) is close to the Kural’s சிற்றினம், and both verses contrast avoiding the low with seeking the noble.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus has his crew stop their ears with wax and has himself bound to the mast so he cannot follow the Sirens’ call.
greek_mythology.explanation: The wise hero knows how strong a corrupting pull can be, so he protects himself from it in advance instead of trusting his willpower.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s point that greatness ‘fears’ low company. Being wary of it is wisdom, not weakness.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The Sirens are a lethal temptation, not petty companions; only the idea of fearful avoidance carries over.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For be assured that if a person be ever so sound himself, yet, if his companion be infected, he who converses with him will be infected likewise.”
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus tells the student to avoid vulgar gatherings, because even a sound person catches the sickness of the company they keep.
philosophy.tie_back: This explains why the great fear mean company: in both texts, closeness to the base is contagious.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong match; wording follows the Carter translation (MIT Classics Archive).

kurals.tamil:
நிலத்தியல்பால் நீர்திரிந் தற்றாகும் மாந்தர்க்கு
இனத்தியல்ப தாகும் அறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Nilaththiyalbaal neerthirindhu atraakum maandharkku
Inaththiyalba thaagum arivu.
kurals.meaning: Just as water changes its nature according to the soil it flows through, a person’s understanding takes on the nature of the company they keep.
kurals.elementary: Rain is pure when it falls, but it turns muddy, salty or sweet depending on the ground it runs over. Our minds work the same way: they pick up the colour and taste of the people we spend time with.
kurals.university: The simile works because rain is pure when it falls and only takes on colour, salt or sweetness from the ground (நிலத்தியல்பு) it touches. அறிவு here is not raw intelligence but practical understanding, the judgement a person brings to life. Valluvar’s claim is environmental: the mind is not a sealed container but something that absorbs from its surroundings. The next two couplets (453–454) sharpen this into a paradox: intelligence seems to belong to the mind but is actually supplied by one’s company.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Queen Kaikeyi loves Rama as her own son, until her hunchbacked maid Manthara keeps working on her mind and turns her into the one who demands Rama’s exile.
hinduism.explanation: A noble queen’s judgement is changed not by her own nature but by the constant presence of a petty, scheming companion.
hinduism.tie_back: Kaikeyi is the water and Manthara is the soil. Her ‘arivu’ took on the nature of the company she kept.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Classic illustration of this exact point; narrative summary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Be not deceived: evil communications corrupt good manners.”
christianity.explanation: Paul quotes a proverb (from the Greek poet Menander) warning that bad company corrupts good character.
christianity.tie_back: Both claim that one’s inner character takes on the quality of one’s company, however good it started out.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend. He led me away from the remembrance after it had come to me.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement the wrongdoer regrets a friendship that pulled him away from guidance he had already received.
islam.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point seen from the end: understanding the person once had was reshaped by a bad friend.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong thematic match; framed as eschatological regret.

judaism.quote_or_event: Maimonides writes that it is human nature to be drawn after the views and deeds of one’s friends and neighbours, so one should keep company with the righteous and the wise and stay away from the wicked.
judaism.explanation: Maimonides treats social influence as a law of human nature and builds a rule of conduct on it.
judaism.tie_back: This is almost the Kural’s thesis in legal prose: character follows company the way water follows soil.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; the concept is a near-exact match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha compares following a fool to wrapping a rotten fish in a blade of kusa grass: the grass itself comes to smell rotten. Leaves wrapped around incense, by contrast, come to smell sweet.
buddhism.explanation: What we are wrapped up with passes its quality to us, whether that is foul or fragrant.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the same image-logic as the Kural. The grass, like the water, takes on the character of what it is in contact with.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrased simile; close parallel in form and meaning.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’s men enter Circe’s hall, share her food and drink, and are turned into swine, keeping only their human minds.
greek_mythology.explanation: Often read allegorically (for example by the Stoics and later moralists) as the way a degrading environment turns people into beasts.
greek_mythology.tie_back: In both, the surroundings a person enters change what they become.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The allegorical reading supports the parallel; the myth itself involves magic, not companionship.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “For from the good you will learn what is good, but if you mix with the bad you will lose the intelligence which you already have.”
philosophy.explanation: Socrates quotes the poet Theognis, who says that good company teaches goodness while bad company destroys the intelligence one already has.
philosophy.tie_back: Theognis’s ‘intelligence’ corresponds exactly to the Kural’s அறிவு, which company can raise or ruin.
philosophy.source: Theognis, as quoted in Plato, Meno 95d (trans. Jowett)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Near one-to-one match, including the specific focus on intelligence.

kurals.tamil:
மனத்தானாம் மாந்தர்க் குணர்ச்சி இனத்தானாம்
இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaththaanaam maandhark kunarchchi inaththaanaam
Innaan enappadunj chol.
kurals.meaning: A person’s perception comes from their own mind, but the verdict “he is such-and-such a man” comes from the company they keep.
kurals.elementary: What you think and feel comes from inside you. But what other people say about you, like ‘he’s a good guy’ or ‘he’s trouble’, mostly depends on who your friends are.
kurals.university: The couplet sets inner and outer against each other: உணர்ச்சி (perception, awareness) arises from மனம் (mind), while reputation, இன்னான் எனப்படுஞ் சொல் (‘the word by which one is called such a man’), arises from இனம் (one’s group). This is a sociological observation: others cannot see into a person’s mind, so they judge by association. Valluvar does not call this judgement unfair. He treats it as a fact the prudent must reckon with, which is why the chapter sits in the Porul (polity) book rather than Aram. Together with 454 it forms a two-step argument: first reputation, then even inner wisdom, turns out to depend on one’s company.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Karna is generous, brave and bound by his word, yet because he stands with Duryodhana’s faction he is remembered as part of the Kaurava wrong and dies on its side.
hinduism.explanation: His personal nobility could not override the name that came from the company he chose.
hinduism.tie_back: Karna’s உணர்ச்சி came from his own mind, but his இன்னான் (‘what kind of man he is’) was settled by his association with Duryodhana.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Interpretive narrative summary; a widely drawn lesson from Karna’s story.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Behold a man gluttonous, and a winebibber, a friend of publicans and sinners.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus’s critics judge him by the people he eats with. Jesus quotes the accusation to show how such people think, and does not accept it.
christianity.tie_back: This confirms the Kural’s observation that society labels a person by their company. The Gospel, however, rejects the verdict when the purpose of the company is redemptive.
christianity._accuracy_note: Confirms the social mechanism but challenges its fairness; a partial and contrasting parallel.

islam.quote_or_event: “A man follows the religion of his friend; so each one should consider whom he makes his friend.”
islam.explanation: The Prophet says a person’s way of life can be read from their close friends, so friends should be chosen with care.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural, it says a person’s identity is judged by, and actually shaped by, their companions.

judaism.quote_or_event: The Mishnah’s saying “woe to the wicked, woe to his neighbour” is applied by Rashi to the tribe of Reuben, who camped beside Korah and were drawn into his rebellion.
judaism.explanation: Being near the wicked brings both ruin and a shared name.
judaism.tie_back: Reuben is remembered alongside Korah because of whom they camped beside, which illustrates the Kural’s point about reputation from company.
judaism._accuracy_note: Focuses on shared harm as much as reputation; moderate match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: The Buddha warns Sigala that one who associates with evil companions finds that gamblers, libertines, drunkards, cheats, swindlers and ruffians become his friends and companions.
buddhism.explanation: Among the dangers of bad company, the Buddha lists that one’s whole circle, and so one’s standing, is defined by such people.
buddhism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s point that one comes to be counted as ‘such a man’ by the circle one keeps.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; about the consequences of bad company, with the reputation angle only implied.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Odysseus returns, the goatherd Melanthius and the disloyal maidservants, who had sided with the suitors, share the suitors’ punishment.
greek_mythology.explanation: They are judged not by their rank but by the camp they joined.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s view that the world pronounces its verdict on a person according to their company.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates judgement by association; harsher and more punitive than the Kural’s point about reputation.

philosophy.quote_or_event: The orator Aeschines reminds the Athenian jury that they put Socrates to death because he was shown to have educated Critias, one of the Thirty Tyrants.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates’s public name was shaped by his association with notorious pupils, whatever his own inner philosophy.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a historical case of the Kural’s claim: people read one’s mind from one’s company.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; strong illustration of reputation by association.

kurals.tamil:
மனத்து ளதுபோலக் காட்டி ஒருவற்கு
இனத்துள தாகும் அறிவு.
kurals.transliteration:
Manaththu ladhupolak kaatti oruvarku
Inaththu ladhaagum arivu.
kurals.meaning: Wisdom appears to belong to a person’s own mind, but it really resides in the company they keep.
kurals.elementary: We think our good sense is all our own. But look closely and much of it comes from the people around us: what they talk about, what they value, how they act.
kurals.university: காட்டி (‘making it appear’) is the key word. Valluvar grants that wisdom seems to live in one’s own mind, then corrects the appearance: it is actually இனத்துளது, lodged in one’s group. This is a strikingly early statement of what is now called distributed or socially embedded cognition: judgement is sustained by the conversations, norms and examples of a circle. It does not deny individual minds, which 453 affirmed, but it undercuts the pride of thinking oneself self-sufficient. The practical corollary, drawn out in 455–460, is that choosing one’s company is choosing one’s wisdom.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Duryodhana relies on his uncle Shakuni’s counsel. The plan of the rigged dice game, which leads to the Pandavas’ exile and in the end to the war, is Shakuni’s idea.
hinduism.explanation: Duryodhana’s ‘wisdom’ in the crisis is really his adviser’s cunning working through him.
hinduism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that what looks like a person’s own mind is supplied by their circle.

christianity.quote_or_event: “The disciple is not above his master: but every one that is perfect shall be as his master.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus says a student, once fully trained, becomes like the one he learns from.
christianity.tie_back: In both, a person’s wisdom takes on the shape of the company they learn from.
christianity._accuracy_note: Teacher-disciple framing rather than peer company; the principle of formation by company is shared.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that the believer is a mirror to his fellow believer.
islam.explanation: A good companion shows you your faults and virtues, so self-knowledge comes through others.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that clear understanding is received from one’s company rather than produced in isolation.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; related but focused on mutual correction rather than the source of wisdom.

judaism.quote_or_event: Rabbi Hanina says he learned much from his teachers, more from his colleagues, and most of all from his students.
judaism.explanation: The Talmud locates the growth of wisdom in the web of people one studies with.
judaism.tie_back: This confirms the Kural’s point that wisdom lives within one’s company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should one find a man who points out faults and who reproves, let him follow such a wise and sagacious person as one would a guide to hidden treasure.”
buddhism.explanation: Wisdom is found by keeping company with the wise, who show one what one cannot see alone.
buddhism.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s point that true understanding comes from the company one keeps.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Positive framing (seeking the wise); the underlying idea matches.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Athena, disguised as Mentor, travels with young Telemachus and guides him to Nestor and Menelaus. In their company the hesitant boy grows into a prudent young man.
greek_mythology.explanation: Telemachus’s new judgement is formed through his companions.
greek_mythology.tie_back: His wisdom seems to be his own but comes from his company, just as in the Kural.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Positive illustration; divine guidance adds a layer the Kural lacks.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus warns that a person who often talks with others must either become like them or bring them round to his own ways.
philosophy.explanation: Conversation is formative, so an untrained mind is reshaped by the company it keeps.
philosophy.tie_back: This supports the Kural’s claim that what passes for one’s own mind is largely the imprint of one’s circle.

kurals.tamil:
மனந்தூய்மை செய்வினை தூய்மை இரண்டும்
இனந்தூய்மை தூவா வரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mananthooimai seivinai thooimai irandum
Inanthooimai thoovaa varum.
kurals.meaning: Purity of mind and purity of deeds both come about through the purity of one’s company.
kurals.elementary: Having a clean heart and doing clean, honest things are both easier when the people around you are good. Good friends act like a support that keeps your thoughts and actions straight.
kurals.university: தூவா (‘support, prop, means’) is the pivot. Purity of mind (மனம்) and of action (செய்வினை), the two pillars of Aram, are made to depend on a third thing, purity of company (இனம்). This goes a step beyond 452’s simile: company is not just an influence on character but its enabling support. The triple repetition of தூய்மை holds the three purities together in one sound-chain, mirroring the argument. Parimelazhagar notes that although mind and deed seem to be individual possessions, they are sustained by one’s associates.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Narada Bhakti Sutra 44 explains why bad company must be shunned: it gives rise to lust, anger and delusion, then loss of memory and of discernment, and finally utter ruin.
hinduism.explanation: The sutra traces a chain from bad association to the collapse of inner purity and so of right action.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the reverse of the Kural’s claim: impure company corrupts mind and deed, just as pure company supports them.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Strong conceptual match; paraphrased because English renderings vary.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Make no friendship with an angry man; and with a furious man thou shalt not go: Lest thou learn his ways, and get a snare to thy soul.”
christianity.explanation: Friendship with a hot-tempered person teaches you his ways and traps your soul.
christianity.tie_back: The same logic runs through both: the company one keeps shapes one’s inner state (soul) and outer conduct (ways).
christianity._accuracy_note: Close; both inner and outer purity are at stake.

islam.quote_or_event: “…the one who is blowing a pair of bellows will either burn your clothes or you will get a bad smell from him.”
islam.explanation: In the Prophet’s parable, an evil companion is like a blacksmith: you come away either scorched or carrying his foul smell.
islam.tie_back: In both, impurity passes from companion to person, staining conduct (the burnt clothes) and inner character (the smell).
islam._accuracy_note: The negative half of the perfume-seller/blacksmith hadith (sunnah.com rendering); strong match.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I have not sat with vain persons, neither will I go in with dissemblers. I have hated the congregation of evil doers; and will not sit with the wicked. I will wash mine hands in innocency.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist links his ‘clean hands’ (pure deeds) directly to his refusal to sit among evildoers.
judaism.tie_back: This mirrors the Kural’s logic: purity of action rests on purity of company.
judaism._accuracy_note: Close match; makes the same link between company and clean deeds.

buddhism.quote_or_event: Prince Ajatasattu, won over by the ambitious monk Devadatta, is persuaded to seize the throne from his father, King Bimbisara, who then dies in prison, while Devadatta plots against the Buddha himself.
buddhism.explanation: A royal heir’s mind and deeds are corrupted through one bad association, ending in patricide.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s claim in its darkest form: impure company brings impurity of mind and of deed.
buddhism.source: Vinaya Pitaka, Cullavagga VII; cf. Digha Nikaya 2

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Odysseus’s scouts eat the lotus offered by the Lotus-eaters, lose all wish to return home, and have to be dragged back to the ships.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sharing the ways of a certain people dissolves both their purpose (mind) and their duty (action).
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates how company undermines both of the purities the Kural names.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: The drug, not the people, is the direct agent; a loose parallel.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “I come home more greedy, more ambitious, more voluptuous, and even more cruel and inhuman, — because I have been among human beings.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca confesses that mixing with the crowd leaves him morally worse in both desire and conduct.
philosophy.tie_back: This is a first-person witness to the Kural’s claim that purity of mind and of action depend on one’s company.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7 (trans. Gummere)

kurals.tamil:
மனந்தூயார்க் கெச்சம்நன் றாகும் இனந்தூயார்க்
கில்லைநன் றாகா வினை.
kurals.transliteration:
Mananthooyaark kechcham nanraagum inanthooyaark
Killai nanraakaa vinai.
kurals.meaning: The pure-minded leave behind a good legacy, and those whose company is pure do no deed that is not good.
kurals.elementary: People with clean hearts leave good things behind them: good children, a good name. People whose friends are good never end up doing bad things, because their friends keep them on track.
kurals.university: எச்சம் (‘that which remains’) is read by Parimelazhagar as good progeny, and by others as the good name that outlives a person; both senses make purity of mind a matter of legacy. The second line is sharper: for those with pure company there is no deed that is not good (இல்லை நன்றாகா வினை). The double negative is emphatic. Good company does not merely encourage good action; it rules out bad action. The couplet divides the labour: the mind decides what one leaves behind, and company decides what one does.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that a sincere seeker who falls short in this life is reborn into a family of the pure and prosperous, or even into a family of wise yogis.
hinduism.explanation: Purity of mind is rewarded with a good lineage and a good circle in which to continue.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s link between a pure mind and a good ‘eccham’ (continuation or posterity).
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; rebirth framing differs from the Kural’s this-worldly legacy.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even so every good tree bringeth forth good fruit; but a corrupt tree bringeth forth evil fruit. A good tree cannot bring forth evil fruit.”
christianity.explanation: Jesus teaches that what a person produces flows from what they are.
christianity.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that a pure source leaves good fruit, and its double negative (‘cannot bring forth evil fruit’).
christianity._accuracy_note: Matches the first line and the emphatic negative; lacks the company element.

islam.quote_or_event: The Prophet taught that when a person dies, their deeds end except for three: ongoing charity, beneficial knowledge, or a righteous child who prays for them.
islam.explanation: A good legacy (the righteous child, lasting good) continues after death.
islam.tie_back: This corresponds closely to Parimelazhagar’s reading of எச்சம் as good progeny.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; matches the legacy half of the couplet.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Blessed is the man that feareth the LORD… His seed shall be mighty upon earth: the generation of the upright shall be blessed.”
judaism.explanation: The upright leave a blessed posterity behind them.
judaism.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that the pure-minded leave a good எச்சம்.
judaism._accuracy_note: Matches the first line; does not address company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If with a pure mind a person speaks or acts happiness follows him like his never-departing shadow.”
buddhism.explanation: Deeds done from a pure mind leave an unbroken trail of good results.
buddhism.tie_back: Both texts see a pure mind as producing lasting good consequences.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Strong on purity of mind; silent on company.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: The pious old couple Baucis and Philemon welcome disguised gods. Their cottage becomes a temple, and at death they are turned into an intertwined oak and linden that are honoured ever after.
greek_mythology.explanation: Pure hearts leave a lasting and venerated legacy.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s ‘eccham’, the good that outlives the pure-minded.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Legacy theme matches; the company dimension is absent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “The friendship of good men is good, being augmented by their companionship.”
philosophy.explanation: Aristotle says good men grow better together, taking on from each other the traits they admire, whereas bad men become worse by growing alike.
philosophy.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s second line: those in good company are held to good action.
philosophy.source: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics IX.12 (trans. W. D. Ross)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Strong on the company half; Ross translation.

kurals.tamil:
மனநலம் மன்னுயிர்க் காக்கம் இனநலம்
எல்லாப் புகழுந் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Mananalam mannuyirk kaakkam inanalam
Ellaap pugazhum tharum.
kurals.meaning: Goodness of mind brings prosperity to a person, and goodness of company brings every kind of renown.
kurals.elementary: A good heart helps you do well in life. But good friends give you something extra: they help people everywhere know and respect you.
kurals.university: Here the parallelism moves from purity (தூய்மை) to goodness (நலம்), and the rewards from legacy to worldly outcomes: ஆக்கம் (prosperity, growth) from the mind, எல்லாப் புகழும் (every kind of fame) from company. The word எல்லா (‘all’) quietly ranks the second above the first. Prosperity may be private, but fame is by nature social and so depends on one’s circle. The couplet explains why reputation, discussed in 453, is not just vanity: in the Porul context of kingship and public life, renown is a resource, and it flows through association.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Vibhishana, righteous in mind, leaves his brother Ravana’s court and takes refuge with Rama. Through that company he wins the throne of Lanka and lasting honour as a model devotee.
hinduism.explanation: His goodness of mind was real, but his renown came through the company he joined.
hinduism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s two rewards exactly: mind gives worth, and company gives fame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marvelled; and they took knowledge of them, that they had been with Jesus.”
christianity.explanation: Ordinary fishermen are recognised and honoured because of the company they had kept.
christianity.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that goodness of company confers renown.
christianity._accuracy_note: Close match on recognition through association.

islam.quote_or_event: “And the first forerunners [in the faith] among the Muhajireen and the Ansar and those who followed them with good conduct — Allah is pleased with them and they are pleased with Him.”
islam.explanation: The early community, and those who followed them in goodness, are honoured as a group.
islam.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s idea that honour comes through belonging to a good company.
islam._accuracy_note: Divine approval rather than worldly fame; partial match.

judaism.quote_or_event: Ruth the Moabite binds herself to Naomi (‘whither thou goest, I will go’), joins Naomi’s people, and becomes the great-grandmother of King David.
judaism.explanation: Her loyal goodness, joined to a good household, led to a renowned lineage.
judaism.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s claim that goodness of company brings renown.
judaism._accuracy_note: Narrative summary; the renown comes through lineage as well as company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Admirable friendship, admirable companionship, admirable camaraderie is actually the whole of the holy life.”
buddhism.explanation: When Ananda suggests that good friendship is half of the spiritual life, the Buddha corrects him: it is the whole.
buddhism.tie_back: Like the Kural, it treats good company as the source of every good, not just a helpful extra.
buddhism.source: Upaddha Sutta, Samyutta Nikaya 45.2 (trans. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Spiritual fulfilment rather than fame; the ‘all’ emphasis matches.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Patroclus, the companion of Achilles, wins lasting fame in the Iliad; his name is bound up with that of the greatest of the Achaeans.
greek_mythology.explanation: His glory is closely tied to the company he kept.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural’s point that renown flows through good association.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrative; Patroclus’s fame also rests on his own deeds.

philosophy.quote_or_event: “Associate with those who will make a better man of you. Welcome those whom you yourself can improve.”
philosophy.explanation: Seneca tells Lucilius to choose companions who raise him up.
philosophy.tie_back: This shares the Kural’s view that goodness of company is a source of advancement.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius 7 (trans. Gummere)
philosophy._accuracy_note: About moral betterment, not renown; partial match.

kurals.tamil:
மனநலம் நன்குடைய ராயினும் சான்றோர்க்கு
இனநலம் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Mananalam nankudaiya raayinum saanrorkku
Inanalam emaap pudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: Even for the wise, who already have fine goodness of mind, good company is a source of security and strength.
kurals.elementary: Even very good and wise people still need good friends. Good company works like a protective wall that keeps their goodness safe.
kurals.university: The concessive ஆயினும் (‘even though’) blocks the obvious objection: surely the already-good (சான்றோர்) do not need company? Valluvar replies that for them too, இனநலம் is ஏமாப்பு, security or fortification. The word suggests protection against the slow wearing-down of virtue by circumstance. Virtue, on this view, is not a fixed possession but a condition to be kept up, and company is part of the upkeep. The couplet guards against the moral self-sufficiency that 454 already undercut.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Arjuna, the greatest archer of his age and a man of dharma, collapses into confusion on the battlefield and is restored only by Krishna, who rides beside him as charioteer and friend.
hinduism.explanation: Even the most capable and righteous hero needs a steadying companion at the decisive moment.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s point that good company is a fortress even for the good.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Narrative framing of the Gita; strong illustration.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And let us consider one another to provoke unto love and to good works: Not forsaking the assembling of ourselves together.”
christianity.explanation: Believers, including the mature, are to keep gathering so they can spur each other to goodness.
christianity.tie_back: In both texts even the virtuous need a good community to support their goodness.

islam.quote_or_event: “And keep yourself patient [by being] with those who call upon their Lord in the morning and the evening, seeking His countenance.”
islam.explanation: Even the Prophet, the best-minded of men, is told to stay in the company of sincere worshippers and not follow the heedless.
islam.tie_back: This is a direct parallel to ‘even for the wise, good company is a fortress’.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match; addressed to the Prophet himself.

judaism.quote_or_event: Honi the Circle-Maker, a holy man, sleeps for seventy years. When he wakes, no one recognises or respects him, and he prays for death. The Talmud concludes: ‘either companionship or death’.
judaism.explanation: Even a saint cannot flourish without a fitting circle.
judaism.tie_back: This makes the Kural’s point in its strongest form: even the virtuous depend on good company.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Should a seeker not find a companion who is better or equal, let him resolutely pursue a solitary course; there is no fellowship with the fool.”
buddhism.explanation: The committed seeker should look for good or better companions, and prefer solitude to a foolish one.
buddhism.tie_back: This shares the Kural’s high valuation of good company and its rejection of bad. It differs in allowing solitude as an alternative.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Partly contrasting: solitude is accepted as a fallback.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: When Diomedes volunteers for the night raid on the Trojan camp, he asks for a companion, saying that when two go together one sees before the other what is best. He chooses Odysseus.
greek_mythology.explanation: Even the bravest hero knows that a good companion multiplies judgement and safety.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This fits the Kural’s ‘fortress’ of good company, even for the excellent.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Aristotle argues that even the supremely happy good man needs friends, since no one would choose to have all goods on condition of being alone. Man is a political creature whose nature is to live with others.
philosophy.explanation: Self-sufficiency does not remove the need for good company, even at the height of virtue.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same claim as the Kural: even the sanror are fortified by good company.

kurals.tamil:
மனநலத்தின் ஆகும் மறுமைமற் றஃதும்
இனநலத்தின் ஏமாப் புடைத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Mananalaththin aakum marumaimat rahdhum
Inanalaththin emaap pudaiththu.
kurals.meaning: Bliss in the world to come is gained through goodness of mind, and even that is made secure by goodness of company.
kurals.elementary: A good heart earns you happiness after this life. But good friends make that happiness even more certain by helping you stay good all the way through.
kurals.university: The previous couplet made good company a fortress for virtue in this life; this one extends the claim to மறுமை, the next world. Even the reward that seems most purely individual, earned by one’s own inner goodness (மனநலம்), is secured (ஏமாப்பு, repeated from 458) by one’s company. The மற்று… அஃதும் (‘and even that’) is emphatic. The pairing of 458 and 459 moves from this world to the next and leaves no domain where company does not matter.

hinduism.quote_or_event: “satsaṅgatve nissaṅgatvaṃ nissaṅgatve nirmohatvam | nirmohatve niścalatattvaṃ niścalatattve jīvanmuktiḥ”
hinduism.explanation: Shankara’s verse traces a chain: from good company comes detachment, from detachment freedom from delusion, from that steadiness in truth, and from that liberation.
hinduism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s claim that the highest spiritual attainment is secured through good company.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Sanskrit original quoted; the English gloss is a standard rendering.

christianity.quote_or_event: “And Jesus said unto him, Verily I say unto thee, To day shalt thou be with me in paradise.”
christianity.explanation: The repentant thief, crucified next to Jesus, turns to him and receives the promise of paradise in his company.
christianity.tie_back: Salvation here comes through a change of heart and is sealed by the company he is with, which parallels the Kural.
christianity._accuracy_note: Grace-centred theology differs; the company element is present.

islam.quote_or_event: When a man asked the Prophet when the Hour would come, the Prophet asked what he had prepared for it. The man said only his love of Allah and His Messenger, and the Prophet replied that he would be with those he loved.
islam.explanation: The company one loves in this life decides one’s company in the next.
islam.tie_back: This is close to the Kural’s claim that good company secures the afterlife.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Then they that feared the LORD spake often one to another: and the LORD hearkened, and heard it, and a book of remembrance was written before him for them that feared the LORD.”
judaism.explanation: The fellowship of the God-fearing is itself recorded for their future reward.
judaism.tie_back: This links good company to one’s standing in the world to come, as the Kural does.
judaism._accuracy_note: Eschatological framing matches; less explicit about company securing virtue.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Not to associate with fools, to associate with the wise, and to honor those who are worthy of honor — this is the highest blessing.”
buddhism.explanation: The Mangala Sutta puts right association first in its ladder of blessings, which ends in the realisation of Nibbana.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the path to the ultimate good begins with and is secured by good company.
buddhism.source: Mangala Sutta, Khuddakapatha 5 / Sutta Nipata 2.4 (trans. Narada Thera)

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Proteus tells Menelaus that he will not die in Argos but be taken to the Elysian plain, because he is Helen’s husband and so son-in-law of Zeus.
greek_mythology.explanation: A blessed afterlife granted because of whom one is joined to.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is a near-literal case of the next world secured by association, though it is kinship, not moral company.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; association here is by marriage rather than goodness.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates, facing death, says that if death leads to a place where he can talk with Orpheus, Musaeus, Hesiod and Homer, he would be willing to die again and again.
philosophy.explanation: For Socrates, the good of the next world is largely the company of the good and wise.
philosophy.tie_back: This echoes the Kural’s link between the afterlife and good company.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase; company is the reward here, not the thing that secures it.

kurals.tamil:
நல்லினத்தி னூங்குந் துணையில்லை தீயினத்தின்
அல்லற் படுப்பதூஉம் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Nallinaththin oongum thunaiyillai theeyinaththin
Allar paduppadhooum il.
kurals.meaning: There is no greater help than good company, and nothing causes more affliction than bad company.
kurals.elementary: Good friends are the best help you can ever have. Bad friends are the worst trouble you can ever have. Nothing else comes close in either direction.
kurals.university: The chapter ends with a symmetrical superlative: nothing surpasses (ஊங்கு) good company as a support (துணை), and nothing causes as much suffering (அல்லல்) as bad company. The emphatic lengthening in படுப்பதூஉம் (an alapedai, or metrical vowel extension) stresses the second half, so the warning weighs more than the praise, in keeping with the chapter title. The couplet sums up the whole adhikaram and connects it to chapter 45: seek the great, avoid the small, because nothing else in life has as much power to help or harm.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Hitopadesha, a deer befriends a smooth-talking jackal against the advice of his true friend, the crow. The jackal leads him into a hunter’s snare, and only the crow’s cleverness saves him.
hinduism.explanation: The fable sets the true friend’s help against the false friend’s harm.
hinduism.tie_back: This illustrates both halves of the Kural: good company is the greatest help and bad company the greatest danger.

christianity.quote_or_event: “He that walketh with wise men shall be wise: but a companion of fools shall be destroyed.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb sets out both outcomes: wisdom from wise company and ruin from foolish company.
christianity.tie_back: Its two-part structure mirrors the Kural’s two-part verdict.

islam.quote_or_event: “Close friends, that Day, will be enemies to each other, except for the righteous.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgement, friendships built on wrongdoing turn into enmity, while righteous friendships last.
islam.tie_back: Both texts say bad company brings the greatest harm and good company the most lasting support.
islam._accuracy_note: Strong match, set in an eschatological frame.

judaism.quote_or_event: Nittai of Arbel taught: keep far from an evil neighbour, do not attach yourself to the wicked, and do not give up belief in retribution.
judaism.explanation: The Mishnah’s ethical teaching warns against closeness to the wicked because of the calamity it brings.
judaism.tie_back: This matches the Kural’s warning that bad company brings more suffering than anything else.
judaism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Sefaria translation; strong match.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Association with fools is ever painful, like partnership with an enemy. But association with the wise is happy, like meeting one’s own kinsmen.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha compares the pain of foolish company with the joy of wise company.
buddhism.tie_back: This is a two-sided verdict matching the Kural almost exactly.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Stranded on Thrinacia, Odysseus’s crew follow Eurylochus’s bad counsel and slaughter the cattle of Helios. Zeus destroys the ship and all of them; only Odysseus, who refused, survives.
greek_mythology.explanation: Following a bad companion’s lead brings total ruin.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This illustrates the Kural’s second half: nothing afflicts like bad company.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Illustrates the negative half; the positive half is only implied.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Socrates asks Meletus whether it is not true that the good do good to those near them and the evil do evil, and whether anyone would rather be harmed than helped by those he lives with.
philosophy.explanation: Socrates takes it as obvious that one’s companions are the nearest source of both benefit and harm.
philosophy.tie_back: This is the same two-sided principle as the Kural.
